analysis.one_liner: Orders refunds, with interest, for electricity charges regulators deemed unjust and unreasonable.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and died in the Senate Energy Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2000–2001 West Coast electricity crisis, wholesale power prices spiked and regulators later questioned many of the charges. This bill would have amended the Federal Power Act to require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, within 60 days of enactment, to order refunds for the portion of electricity transmission and sales charges it judged unjust or unreasonable — with interest — for charges paid between June 1, 2000 and June 19, 2001 [S2][S3]. It was introduced by Senator Barbara Boxer of California on June 20, 2001, referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Electricity customers who paid inflated wholesale power charges during the period the bill covered — most directly Californians, whose utilities bought power at record prices during the 2000–2001 crisis and passed much of those costs on through bills and rate increases. The refunds would have included interest from the date charges were paid [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to order a refund, within 60 days of enactment, for the portion of electricity transmission or sales charges it has deemed unjust or unreasonable, with interest from the date the charges were paid [S2][S3].
The refund window covers charges paid between June 1, 2000 and June 19, 2001, capturing the period of the Western electricity price spike [S3][S2].

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity sellers and generators who collected the excess charges would repay them plus interest. Wholesale buyers such as utilities and power marketers would receive the refunds, with the amount reaching retail customers depending on how the money was passed through [S3].

drawbacks.text: Retroactive refunds on a year of transactions could have been fought in court and in agency proceedings, since 'unjust and unreasonable' is a judgment call, delaying or shrinking what customers actually receive.

The money would first flow to wholesale buyers, not directly to households, so the amount reaching retail electricity customers would depend on utility pass-through — a mechanism the bill did not spell out [S3].

The bill sets a hard 60-day deadline for the Commission to act on every charge it has deemed unjust or unreasonable, which an honest supporter would acknowledge is an aggressive timetable for a regulator reviewing complex market data [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to customers who overpaid during the crisis was potentially large and concrete — repayment of excessive charges with interest [S2][S3]. The main costs were procedural and legal: disputes over which charges qualified, the pace of a 60-day mandate, and the fact that refunds route through wholesale buyers rather than straight to households. On balance this was a straightforward relief bill whose main flaw was an optimistic deadline and an indirect delivery path, not its purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer introduced the bill in the Senate on June 20, 2001, and spoke about it in introductory remarks [S5][S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources that same day — its last recorded action [S5][S1].
The committee never held a hearing or reported the bill, and with no further action before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, the bill died without ever coming to a vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale electricity sellers who collected the questioned charges came out ahead: with the bill dead, no statutory refund requirement ever took effect, and customers who overpaid kept carrying those costs. The Senate Energy Committee's inaction preserved that result.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wholesale power sellers kept the excess charges

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was her lone sponsorship with no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Jim Jeffords (I)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 20, 2001 and never held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it out; the bill died there.

against.name: Wholesale electricity generators and traders
against.role: Sellers of wholesale power during the 2000–2001 Western price spike
against.what_they_did: The bill would have forced repayment of excess charges with interest; the industry was the target of refund efforts during the California crisis.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors signed on and no roll-call votes were ever taken, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor; it never became a partisan floor fight.

industries.note: The bill would have required these sellers to refund charges FERC deemed unjust or unreasonable, plus interest, for the June 2000–June 2001 period — money that came largely from California customers during the price spike. Their gain from the bill dying was the public's cost.

industries.industry: Retail electric utilities and wholesale power buyers
industries.note: They would have received the refunds first and, in a crisis year when many passed high wholesale costs to customers, would have been the channel for relief to ratepayers — though the bill did not mandate how refunds reach retail customers.
